title: Declining Prey Size in the Southern African Pleistocene: Evaluating the Human Impact
content: Megafauna extinctions are known from the Late Quaternary. This study analyzes trends in prey size from 184 contexts across 49 archaeological sites in southern Africa to assess changes in prey size during the Pleistocene, including the pre-Late Quaternary transition between the Early Stone Age (ESA) and the Middle Stone Age (MSA). Very large prey (>950kg) accounted for over 34% of the biomass in the ESA, declining to 22% in MSA and 11% in LSA, with a compensatory increase in the contribution of smaller (<295 kg) prey that increased from 7% in the ESA to 37% in the MSA and to 48% in the LSA. These trends persisted even when only non-cave sites were considered. We also hypothesize that targeting fat in prey because of a constraint on protein consumption by humans could have been a causal factor in the decline.
